analysis.one_liner: Requires user consent before websites track or sell your data, and declares that data your property.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on July 2, 2024 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it sat with no cosponsors and no action until the Congress ended on January 3, 2025. [S1][S3][S4]
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it unlawful for websites, apps, and online businesses to use cookies, tracking pixels, or any personal information about you unless you consent first, and they could not cut you off for saying no. Once you do consent, the platform would have to disclose what it collects, what it's worth, and treat that information as your exclusive property. The Federal Trade Commission, state attorneys general, and users themselves could sue to enforce it. [S2]
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary internet users, who today have little practical control over how websites and apps collect, share, and monetize their personal information. [S2]

how_it_helps.text: Bars platforms from using cookies, collecting any information about a user, or delivering personalized content without that user's consent, and prohibits tracking pixels entirely. [S2]
Prohibits platforms from restricting a user's access because the user declined to consent to tracking. [S2]
Requires platforms to treat collected data as the user's exclusive property, disclose its economic value, and notify users of any change in how it is used. [S2]
Gives users a private right of action to sue for damages, with users guaranteed at least 90 percent of total damages, and lets the FTC and state attorneys general enforce the rules. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Digital platforms, advertising businesses, and the data-driven online economy, which would lose the ability to track users and monetize personal information without consent, and which would bear enforcement, disclosure, and damages costs. [S2]

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts state law on these requirements, which could override stronger existing state privacy protections, such as California's, with a single federal standard. [S2]

Requiring every platform to determine and disclose the 'economic value' of each user's information, and treating all data as a user's exclusive property right, is a novel and untested scheme that would be difficult to implement and could invite litigation over how data value is calculated. [S2]

The ban on cookies, pixels, and data sharing without consent would upend the advertising-supported business model behind much of the free internet, raising the question of who pays for online content if ad tracking ends. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protection — no tracking without consent, and no punishment for refusing — addresses a real and widespread problem, and the strong enforcement tools (a private lawsuit with at least 90 percent of damages, plus FTC and state enforcement) give it teeth. But the bill was drafted without the refining process that comes from committee work or cosponsors: federal preemption could wipe out stronger state privacy laws, and the economic-value disclosure and property-right provisions are untested. As written, it is a promising concept with real design risks. [S2]

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, never gained a single cosponsor, and never received a hearing or vote before the two-year Congress ended. [S1][S3][S4]

narrative.text: Representative David Schweikert introduced the User Data Protection Act on July 2, 2024. [S1][S4]
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day; that referral was the only action it ever received. [S4]
No member joined as a cosponsor, and the bill never reached a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025. [S3]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Digital platforms and the online advertising industry, which keep tracking users and monetizing personal data unchanged, at least for now.

for.name: Rep. David Schweikert
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Energy and Commerce Committee. [S1][S4]

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — during the six months it had jurisdiction. [S4]

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors, so no partisan shape can be measured; the sole sponsor was a Republican. [S3]

industries.note: Their revenue depends on tracking users across sites without meaningful consent; the bill outlaws cookies, tracking pixels, and data sharing without permission. Ordinary users' privacy is precisely what these firms monetize. [S2]

industries.industry: Consumer websites, apps, and online businesses
industries.note: They would lose ad-targeting data but gain uniform federal rules; many fund 'free' services through ad tracking, so the bill would force a rethink of how online content is paid for. [S2]
Federal preemption would displace state privacy laws such as California's, which in some respects are stricter. [S2]
